answers.text: When the cellular receptor is bound by the natural ligand, or a drug that mimics the natural ligand, that is the signal for the cell to do something.
The cellular receptors that most of our drugs bind to in order to perform their therapeutic action are involved in communication between other cells or other parts of the body

Cellular receptors can be increased or decreased by the cell, thereby increasing or decreasing the number of messages that to to the cell (provided there are adequate ligands to bind to those receptors).

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No, there are four types of cellular receptors and each type is quite different. For instance, the intracellular receptors are the ones that are acted on by something like a steroidal hormone - and they result in the DNA of the cell increasing the production of proteins. Conversely, some receptors control the channel proteins, and their binding can result in additional influx of the molecules that it is designed to allow into or out of the cell.

behaviour.feedbackOnWrong: Actually, cells often respond to a drug by altering the number of receptors on their surface. This is the reason that some medications can be effective for only a limited duration. For instance, people become tolerant of the effects of opioids due to the fact that the cells downregulate the number of cellular receptors.

params.question: While the cell has the ability to increase or decrease the number of receptors on the surface, it never does this in response to drugs.

behaviour.feedbackOnCorrect: Yes, the ligand is the natural substance for which the receptor is made. For instance insulin is the ligand for insulin receptors. Our medications can mimic the actions of the natural ligand, in which case it is an AGONIST, or it can block the receptor, competing with the natural ligand for the binding spot, in which case it is an antagonist.

params.question: In Pharmacology, when we are discussing cellular receptors, the ligand is the natural substance for which the substance is made, and it can be a small molecule, ion, or protein.
